[p-490 not applicable; the text as given] Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on surah 4, verse 43:

﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: "intoxicated" means intoxicated by wine. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Habib that: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf prepared food and drink and invited a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. They ate and drank until they became intoxicated. Then they put forward 'Umar, and he led them in the Maghrib prayer, and he recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, and you are not worshippers of what I worship, and I am not a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor are you worshippers of what I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾. Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾." The second opinion: "intoxicated" means drowsy from sleep. This is the view of al-Dahhak. The root of "sukr" (intoxication) is "sakr," which means blocking the flow of water; so intoxication from drink blocks the path of understanding.

If it is asked: how is it permissible to forbid one who is intoxicated (from prayer)? There are two answers. The first: he may be intoxicated without reaching a state in which the matter cannot be borne. The second: he was forbidden from exposing himself to intoxication while a prayer was due upon him.

﴿Nor one who is in a state of janabah (ritual impurity), except while passing through, until you wash yourselves﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it means the path of the traveller who is in janabah and does not pray until he performs tayammum (dry ablution). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of Abu Mijlaz from him, and of Mujahid, al-Hakam, and Ibn Zayd. The second: the one in janabah should not approach the places of prayer in the mosques except passing through in transit. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Dahhak and Ibn Yasar from him, and it is the view of Jabir, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, and al-Nakha'i.

﴿And if you are sick﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: whatever is called "sickness," whether harmed by water or not harmed. This is the view of Dawud ibn 'Ali. The second: only that sickness in which the use of water causes harm, not that in which it causes no harm. This is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. The third: only that in which the use of water is feared to cause destruction, not that in which it is not feared. This is the second of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

﴿or on a journey﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: whatever is called "journey," whether short or long. This is the view of Dawud. The second: a distance of one day and night or more. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both. The third: a distance of three days. This is the position of Abu Hanifa.

﴿or one of you comes from the ghait (the toilet)﴾. The ghait is a low-lying place on the ground to which a person would go for his need. The word was used metaphorically to refer to what comes out (of the body), and then its use became frequent until it became like a literal meaning. The evidence that ghait is literally the name of a place and not of what comes out is the verse of the poet:

"Has news of me not reached you, when I am in the ghait calling for help?
And you shouted in the ghait, O wretch!"

﴿or you have touched women﴾. Regarding this there are two readings. One: (lamastum) without an alif, recited by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. The other: ﴿lamastum﴾ with the alif, which is the reading of the rest.

Regarding this "touching," there are two opinions. The first: it means sexual intercourse. This is the view of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid. The second: touching is with the hand, and "contact" (ifda') is with some part of the body. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ubaydah, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata', and Ibn Sirin, and al-Shafi'i said likewise.

Regarding the difference between the two readings "lamastum" and "lamastum" (with the alif), there are two opinions. The first: "lamastum" (with alif) is more emphatic than "lamistum." The second: ﴿lamastum﴾ requires wudu' (ablution) upon both the one who touches and the one who is touched, whereas "lamastum" requires it only upon the one who touches, not the one touched.

﴿and you find no water, then perform tayammum (dry ablution)﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it means worship and seeking (the right thing). This is the view of Sufyan. The second: it means intending (the earth). It is mentioned that in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "then go to clean ground (sa'idan tayyiban)."

Regarding al-sa'id (clean ground) there are four opinions. The first: it is smooth ground on which there is no plant or tree. This is the view of Qatadah. The second: it is level ground. This is the view of Ibn Zayd. The third: it is dust. This is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Shafi'i. The fourth: it is the surface of the earth that has dust and powder. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if, in the forenoon, it throws over the sa'id a beetle with a snout in the bones of the head."

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿tayyiban (clean)﴾ there are four opinions. The first: lawful (halal). This is the view of Sufyan. The second: pure (tahir). This is the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari. The third: the dust of cultivated land. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: it is a place that is sloping and not flat and open. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

﴿So wipe your faces and your hands﴾. The face that is wiped in tayammum is the same as the area delimited in washing for wudu'.

As for wiping the two hands, there are three opinions. The first: the two palms up to the wrists, not the forearms. This is the view of 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Makhul, and Malik said so in one of his two opinions, and al-Shafi'i in his older opinion. The second: the two forearms together with the elbows. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, and al-Shafi'i in his newer opinion. The third: up to the shoulders and the armpits. This is the view of al-Zuhri, and something similar is reported from Abu Bakr.

They differed regarding the permissibility of tayammum in the case of janabah (major ritual impurity), on two opinions. The first: it is permissible. This is the view of the majority. The second: it is not permissible. This is the view of 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Nakha'i.

They differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, on two opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning a group of the Companions who were struck by wounds. This is the view of al-Nakha'i. The second: it was revealed concerning the lack of water during a journey. This is the view of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 44–46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture, how they purchase error?﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: they, by their denial of the attribute of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), have become like one who buys error in exchange for guidance.

The second: they used to give their rabbis their wealth in return for their practice of denying the Messenger (ﷺ). The third: they used to take bribes. Thabit al-Bunani narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) cursed the one who gives a bribe, the one who takes a bribe, and the broker (al-ra'ish), and this is the intermediary between the two.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And hear, but not heard﴾. Regarding this there are two statements. The first: its meaning is "Hear, may you not hear," and this is the saying of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it means "unacceptable from you," and this is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

﴿And [they say], "Ra'ina," distorting with their tongues﴾. Regarding this there are three statements. The first: this word was an insult in their language, so Allah informed His Prophet of it and he forbade them from it.

The second: it used to function as mockery.

The third: it used to come out in a manner of arrogance.

O People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), namely the Jews and the Christians.

﴿Believe in what We have sent down﴾, namely the Qur'an.

﴿confirming what is with you﴾, namely your scriptures.

﴿before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their hinder parts﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: that the obliteration of faces is the erasing of their features until they become like the nape of the neck, and We make their eyes at the back of their heads, so that they walk backwards. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: that We obliterate them from guidance and turn them back upon their hinder parts, meaning in their misguidance, as a rebuke to them, that they will never be fit for anything. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Ibn Abi Najih, and al-Suddi.

﴿Or We curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath﴾, meaning, We transform them into apes. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 4, verses 49–52:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim purity for themselves? Rather, God purifies whom He wills﴾. This refers to the Jews and their claiming purity for themselves. There are four opinions on it:

First: their saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved." This is the view of Qatada and al-Hasan.

Second: their putting forward their children to lead them in prayer, supposing that those children have no sins. This is the view of Mujahid and Ikrima.

Third: their saying, "Our children will seek forgiveness for us and purify us." This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: some of them purifying others in order to gain some of the worldly life through it. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿And they will not be wronged a fatil﴾. Regarding this, there are two opinions:

One: it means the fatil (the thin thread) that is in the split of the date stone. This is the view of Ata', Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and one of the two opinions of Ibn Abbas.

al-Hasan said: the fatil is what is in the inside of the date stone, the naqir (the small pit mark) is what is on its back, and the qitmir (the thin membrane) is its skin.

Two: it means the dirt that is rolled up between the fingers. This is the view of al-Suddi and one of the two opinions of Ibn Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, who believe in jibt and taghut?﴾ Regarding this, there are five opinions:

First: they are two idols that the polytheists used to worship. This is the view of Ikrima.

Second: the jibt are the idols, and the taghut are the interpreters of the idols. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Third: the jibt is magic, and the taghut is the devil. This is the view of Umar and Mujahid.

Fourth: the jibt is the sorcerer, and the taghut is the soothsayer. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Fifth: the jibt is Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the taghut is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This is the view of al-Dahhak.(p-496)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 53–55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom? For then they would not give the people even a speck (naqir)﴾. Concerning the naqir there are three opinions. The first: it is that which is in the back of the date pit (nawah), and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', and al-Dahhak.

The second: it is that which is in the middle of the date pit, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: it is the flick of a man's thing with the tip of his thumb, and this is a narration from Abu al-'Aliyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ He means the Jews.

Concerning the people whom it refers to, there are three opinions. The first: they are the Arabs, and this is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: it refers specifically to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Ikrimah.

The third: they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and this is the saying of some of the later scholars.

Concerning the bounty that was envied, there are two opinions. The first: it is prophethood; they envied the Arabs for having it among them, and this is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: it is his permission for the Prophet (ﷺ) to marry whichever women he wished without limit, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi. (p-497)

﴿We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾. Concerning the great kingdom there are four opinions. The first: it is the kingdom of Sulayman son of Dawud, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: prophethood, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: what they were supported with of angels and armies, and this is the saying of Hammam ibn al-Harith.

The fourth: what Allah permitted to Dawud and Sulayman of women without limit, so that Dawud married ninety-nine women and Sulayman married one hundred women, and this is the saying of al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Our verses — We will drive them into a Fire﴾ up to His saying: ﴿that they may taste the punishment﴾. If it is said: How is it possible that they be given skins other than their skins which they had in the world, so that they are punished in them? For if that were permissible, it would be permissible for them to be given bodies and spirits other than their bodies and spirits which they had in the world; and if that were permissible, it would be permissible that those punished in the Hereafter with the Fire be other than those whom God promised in the world punishment by the Fire for their disbelief.

The scholars have answered this with three answers. The first: the pain of punishment reaches the human being, who is other than the skin and flesh; the skin is only burned so that the pain of punishment may reach the human being, whereas the skin and flesh do not feel pain. Thus it makes no difference whether the disbeliever's own skin is returned to him or other skin.

The second answer: those first skins are returned anew [not] burned.

The third answer: the skins that are returned are only their garments before they were made into clothing for them, and God named them skins. One speaker denied this view, that the skins burn and are returned not burned, because in the period from their burning until their return there would be annihilation of them, and in their annihilation there would be relief, whereas God, may He be exalted, has informed that they neither die nor will the punishment be lightened for them.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 58:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render the trusts to their owners﴾. Regarding who is meant by this, there are four opinions. The first is that it refers to the rulers of the Muslims. This is the view of Shahr ibn Hawshab, Makhul, and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second is that it commands the sultan (ruler) to admonish the women. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with this regarding Uthman ibn Abi Talha, that he should return to him the keys of the Ka'bah. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth is that it applies to everyone entrusted with anything. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

Qatadah narrated from al-Hasan that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Render the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

(p-٤٩٩)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 59:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ means: obey Allah in His commands and His prohibitions, and obey the Messenger.

Al-A'mash narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever obeys me has obeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed Allah, and whoever disobeys my commander has disobeyed me."

Regarding obedience to the Messenger there are two opinions. The first: following his Sunnah (the prophetic practice), and this is the view of Ata'.

The second: "Obey the Messenger" refers to obeying him while he is alive, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Regarding "those in authority" (ulu al-amr) there are four opinions. The first: they are the rulers (umara'), and this is the view of Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

Hisham narrated from Urwah, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "After me there will be governors over you. The righteous among them will govern you by their righteousness, and the wicked among them will govern you by their wickedness. So listen to them and obey them in everything that accords with the truth, pray behind them. If they do good, it is for you and for them; if they do evil, it is for you and against them."

Those who held this view differed concerning the occasion of revelation regarding the rulers. Ibn Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Hudhafah ibn Qays al-Sahmi, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him on an expedition (sariyyah).

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir and Khalid ibn al-Walid, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent the two of them on an expedition.

The second opinion: they are the scholars and jurists, and this is the view of Jabir ibn Abdullah, al-Hasan, Ata', and Abu al-Aliyah.

The third: they are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: they are Abu Bakr and Umar, and this is the view of Ikrimah.

The obedience owed to those in authority is binding only within obedience to Allah, not in disobedience to Him. It is obedience that may cease, since their disobedience is permissible. The obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) may not cease, since disobeying him is impossible.

Nafi' narrated from Abdullah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "It is incumbent upon the Muslim person to obey, in what he loves and in what he dislikes, unless he is commanded to commit disobedience; then there is no obedience."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it means to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger.

﴿If you should believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most favorable in result﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: it is most praiseworthy in outcome; this is the view of Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is more apparent in truth and clearer in correctness; this is the meaning of Mujahid's view.

The third: it is better than your interpretation, which does not return to a foundation and does not lead to truth; this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 60–63:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet they desire to take their disputes to the tyrant (al-taghut), when they were commanded to reject it?﴾ Scholars differed over who this verse was revealed about, in two opinions.

The first: it was revealed about a man from among the hypocrites (munafiqun) and a man from among the Jews, between whom there was a dispute. The Jew said, "Let us take it to the people of your religion, for I know they do not accept bribes," and the hypocrite said, "Let us take it to the Jews, to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf," because he knew that they accepted bribes. So they agreed to take their dispute to a soothsayer (kahin) from Juhayna. Then God revealed this verse about them: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed in what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning the hypocrite, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾, meaning the Jew.

﴿They desire to take their disputes to the tyrant﴾, meaning the soothsayer. This is the opinion of al-Sha'bi and Mujahid.

The second: it was revealed about two men, one from Banu al-Nadir and one from Banu Qurayza. In the Jahiliyya, when Banu Qurayza killed a man from Banu al-Nadir, they would exact retaliation from the killer, but when Banu al-Nadir killed a man from Banu Qurayza, they would not exact retaliation from the killer, and they would give his blood-money as sixty wasqs of dates. When some people from Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir embraced Islam, a man from Banu al-Nadir killed a man from Banu Qurayza, and they brought their dispute to the Prophet ﷺ. The Nadiri said to the Messenger of God, "In the Jahiliyya we used to give them blood-money of sixty wasqs of dates, so we shall give them that today." The Qurayza said, "We are brothers in lineage and religion, and that was only a custom of the Jahiliyya, and now Islam has come." So God, exalted is He, revealed, rebuking them for what they had done: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that a life is for a life﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], then He mentioned the words of Banu al-Nadir: ﴿Do they then desire the judgement of the Jahiliyya?﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 50]. Then he took the Nadiri and killed him in retaliation for the Qurayzi. So Banu al-Nadir and Qurayza boasted to each other and entered Medina, and they took their dispute to Abu Burda al-Aslami, the soothsayer, and God revealed concerning that: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed in what has been revealed to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 60], meaning at present, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾, meaning when they were Jews.

﴿They desire to take their disputes to the tyrant﴾, meaning Abu Burda al-Aslami the soothsayer. This is the opinion of al-Suddi.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when a calamity strikes them﴾, to the end of the verse.

Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions. The first: that Umar killed a hypocrite who had not accepted the judgement of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and his fellow hypocrites came demanding his blood, and they swore by God, "We intended in demanding his blood only good toward the women, and nothing that agrees with the truth in our affair."

The second: that after the retaliation against their companion, the hypocrites apologized to the Messenger of God ﷺ for their resort to other than him in judgement, saying, "We intended in our turning away from you only to bring about reconciliation between the disputants and to do good through leniency in the judgement, not by carrying the bitter truth," so this verse was revealed.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom God knows what is in their hearts﴾, meaning of the hypocrisy which they conceal.

﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾. Regarding the combination of turning away (al-i'rad) and admonition (al-wa'z), despite their apparent incompatibility, there are three aspects. The first: turn away from them with enmity toward them, and admonish them concerning what has appeared from them. The second: turn away from punishing them, and admonish them. The third: turn away from accepting their excuses, and admonish them.

﴿And speak to them, concerning themselves, a far-reaching word﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: that he should say to them, "If you manifest what is in your hearts, he will kill you," for it reaches their souls in every way. This is the opinion of al-Hasan. The second: that he should restrain them from what they are upon with the most effective of deterrents.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 64–65:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that which is in dispute between them﴾. The meaning of ﴿in dispute between them﴾ is: that which has arisen between them of mushajarah (mushajarah: dispute and disagreement). It is called mushajarah because of the interweaving of some of the speech, like the interweaving of trees (shajar) with their branches intertwined.

﴿Then they will not find within themselves any discomfort (haraj) concerning what you have decided﴾. Regarding haraj (haraj: constriction, discomfort) there are two interpretations. One of them: it means doubt, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: it means sin, and this is the saying of al-Dahhak.

There is disagreement about the occasion of its revelation, according to two views.

One of them: it was revealed concerning the hypocrite and the Jew who sought judgment from the tyrant (taghut), and this is the saying of Mujahid and al-Sha'bi.

The second: it was revealed concerning al-Zubayr and a man from the Ansar who had witnessed Badr, who "disputed before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over water channels (shiraj) from the lava field (harrah) that they were using to irrigate palm trees. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Irrigate, O Zubayr, then send the water on to your neighbour). The Ansari became angry and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, [did you rule this way] because he is the son of your paternal aunt?' The face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed color until it was evident that this had grieved him. Then he said: (O Zubayr, hold back the water until it reaches the walls (al-judur) or the ankles (al-ka'bayn), then release the water). So this verse was revealed." This is the saying of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Urwah, and Umm Salamah.

﴿Whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous. How excellent are these as companions.﴾ As for *al-siddiqun*, it is the plural of *siddiq* (one who is exceedingly truthful), and they are the followers of the prophets.

Concerning the naming of the *siddiq*, there are two opinions. The first is that it is a *fi‘𝘪̄l* pattern (intensive form) derived from *al-sidq* (truthfulness). The second is that it is a *fi‘𝘪̄l* pattern derived from *al-ṣadaqah* (charity).

As for *al-shuhada'*, it is the plural of *shahid*, who is one who is killed in the way of Allah, exalted is He.

Concerning the naming of the *shahid*, there are two opinions. The first is that he is so called because he upholds the testimony of the truth, to the point that he is killed in the way of Allah. The second is that he is so called because he witnesses the honour of Allah, exalted is He, in the Hereafter.

He also bears witness over the servants concerning their deeds on the Day of Resurrection, if he is sealed with being killed in the way of Allah. (p-505)

As for *al-salihun*, it is the plural of *salih* (righteous), and concerning it there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to everyone whose deeds are righteous. The second is that it refers to everyone whose inner state and outward conduct are both righteous.

As for *al-rafiq* (companion), concerning it there are two opinions. The first is that it is derived from *al-rifq* (gentleness) in action. The second is that it is derived from *al-rifq* (ease) in travel.

The occasion of revelation of this verse, as related by al-Hasan, Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Rabi‘, and al-Suddi, is that some people imagined that they would not see the prophets in Paradise, because the prophets are in the highest ranks of *‘Illiyyin*. They became saddened and asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 71–74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾ (khudhū ḥidhrakum). There are two opinions regarding it. The first: it means, be wary of your enemy.

The second: its meaning is, take your weapons (silah), and He called it ḥidhr (precaution) because the cautious person protects himself by it.

﴿Then go forth in separate groups or go forth all together.﴾ Al-thubāt is the plural of thubah, and a thubah is a band (ʿuṣbah) of men. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Indeed I go out in the morning with a band of noble men, drunk, yet able to do whatever we wish.*

(p-506)

So the meaning of the verse is: go forth in bands (ʿuṣab), in groups (firaq), or all together.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let those fight in the way of Allah who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter﴾. It means: those who sell the worldly life for the Hereafter. He expressed selling by the word "buying" (shirāʾ).

﴿And whoever fights in the way of Allah and is killed or achieves victory – We will bestow upon him a great reward.﴾ If it is asked: the promise from Allah is for fighting, so how is it made conditional upon being killed or achieving victory? It is said: because fighting generally leads to being killed, so the promise made for fighting becomes a promise for whoever it leads to. And fighting, according to the reward it deserves when it leads to being killed or to victory, is greater; and so He informed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 77–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who were told, "Restrain your hands, establish the prayer, and give the zakat"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a faction of them fear people as they fear Allah, or even with greater fear.﴾ Concerning whom this verse was revealed, there are four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning some of the Companions who asked the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah for permission to fight the polytheists, and he did not permit them. Then, when fighting was prescribed for them while they were in Madinah, a faction of them said what Allah mentioned about them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The third: it was revealed concerning the Jews.

The fourth: it describes the believer, in respect of the fear that human nature has been created with. This is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built high.﴾ Regarding the "towers" (buruj) here, there are three opinions. The first: they are palaces. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: they are palaces in the sky, specifically named by this name. This is the view of al-Suddi and al-Rabi'.

The third: they are the houses that are within fortresses. This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The root meaning of buruj is manifestness, and from it comes tabarruj (display) of a woman when she reveals herself.

Regarding "mushayyadah" (built high) there are three opinions. The first: it means plastered, and shid is plaster (jiss). This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The second: al-Mushayyad is that which is lengthened in height; one says "shada al-rajul binahahu" and "ashadahu" when he raised it. From this comes "ashadtu bi-dhikr al-rajul" when you praise a man and elevate him. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: al-Mushayyad, with the shadda (doubled letter), means lengthened, and with the lightened form, means plastered.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If a good thing befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah"; but if an evil thing befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]."﴾ Concerning those who say this, there are two opinions. One: they are the hypocrites. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: they are the Jews. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Regarding "good" (hasanah) and "evil" (sayyi'ah) here, there are three interpretations. The first: hardship and ease.

The second: fertility and drought. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: victory and defeat. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding His saying ﴿from you﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: meaning, by your poor management. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second: they mean by the ill omen that has befallen us from you, by way of tatayyur (taking omens) with it. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if an evil thing befalls them, they attribute it to Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil reaches you is from yourself.﴾ Scholars differed about the intended addressee of this address, in three opinions.

The first: the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, and he is the one meant.

The second: it is directed to the Prophet ﷺ but the one meant is someone other than him. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is directed to the human being, and its implied meaning is: "Whatever good reaches you, O human, is from Allah." This is the view of Qatadah.

Regarding "good" (hasanah) and "evil" (sayyi'ah) here, there are three opinions. The first: the good is blessing in religion and in this world, and the evil is calamity in religion and in this world. This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The second: the good is what befell him on the day of Badr, and the evil is what befell him on the day of Uhud, namely the wound to his head and the breaking of his incisor. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The third: the good is obedience, and the evil is disobedience. This is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from yourself﴾ has two opinions. The first: meaning, because of your sin.

The second: because of your action.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 80–81:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. It is obedience to Allah only because it agrees with the command of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿But whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. There are two interpretations regarding this:
One of them: meaning, a guardian for them from sins, so that they do not commit them.

The second: a guardian over their deeds for which the recompense is due, so you would fear that you would not be able to uphold them, for Allah, exalted is He, is the One who recompenses for them.

﴿And they say, "Obedience"﴾, meaning the hypocrites, i.e., "Our affair is obedience."

﴿But when they go out from your presence, a group of them plots by night other than what you say﴾. Tabyit (planning by night) is every action that is devised at night. ʿUbayd ibn Hammam said:

They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they plotted, and they had come to me with a disgraceful matter,
To marry their unmarried woman to Mundhir,
And does a free man marry a free woman to a slave?

(p-510)

Regarding the naming of an action done at night as bayat (plotting by night), there are two views: One of them: because the night is the time of lodging (mabit).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 80–81:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. It is obedience to Allah only because it agrees with the command of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿But whoever turns away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. There are two interpretations regarding this:
One of them: meaning, a guardian for them from sins, so that they do not commit them.

The second: a guardian over their deeds for which the recompense is due, so you would fear that you would not be able to uphold them, for Allah, exalted is He, is the One who recompenses for them.

﴿And they say, "Obedience"﴾, meaning the hypocrites, i.e., "Our affair is obedience."

﴿But when they go out from your presence, a group of them plots by night other than what you say﴾. Tabyit (planning by night) is every action that is devised at night. ʿUbayd ibn Hammam said:

They came to me, but I was not pleased with what they plotted, and they had come to me with a disgraceful matter,
To marry their unmarried woman to Mundhir,
And does a free man marry a free woman to a slave?

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 82–83:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ The root of tadabbur (reflection) is dabbur (the back of a thing), because it is looking into the consequences of matters.

﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much inconsistency.﴾ Regarding "inconsistency" here there are three opinions. The first: contradiction between truth and falsehood; this is the saying of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. (p-511)

The second: between eloquent and contemptible (speech); this is the saying of some of the Basrans.

The third: that it means inconsistency in reports about what they conceal; this is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter of security or fear, they spread it around.﴾ Regarding who is meant by this there are two opinions. One: the hypocrites; this is the saying of Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak.

The second: that they are the weak among the Muslims; this is the saying of al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj.

﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger and to those of authority among them⦆ Regarding "those of authority among them" there are three opinions. The first: that they are the commanders; this is the saying of Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

The second: they are the commanders of the expeditions (sarayا).

The third: they are the people of knowledge and jurisprudence; this is the saying of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Juraij, Ibn Najih and al-Zajjaj.

﴿would have known it from those among them who derive it⦆ Regarding them there are two opinions. One: that they are those in authority. The second: that they are the hypocrites or the weak among the Muslims who were addressed at the beginning of the verse. The meaning of yastanbitunahu ("derive it") is: they extract it, taken from istinbat al-ma' (extracting water), and from it the Nabat were so named because of their extracting of springs.

﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except for a few.﴾ Regarding "the bounty of Allah" here there are three opinions. The first: it means the Prophet ﷺ. The second: the Qur'an.

The third: subtle kindness and divine success (tawfiq).

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿you would have followed Satan, except for a few﴾ there are four opinions. The first: it means you would have followed Satan, except for a few of you, for he (the one who did not follow Satan) was not following him.

The second: "they would have known it from those who derive it, except for a few of you"; this is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah. (p-512)

The third: "they spread it around, except for a few"; this is the saying of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "you would have followed Satan, except for a few, while still following him."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 84–87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will have a share of its burden﴾. Regarding the good intercession and the evil intercession there are two opinions. The first: it is a person's request on behalf of his companion, that he may obtain good through his request or evil through his request. This is the saying of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: the good intercession is supplication for the believers, and the evil intercession is supplication against them, because the Jews used to do that, so Allah threatened them for it.

Regarding al-kifl (share, portion) there are two interpretations. One: it is the burden and the sin, and this is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: it is the portion, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 28]. This is the saying of al-Suddi, al-Rabi', and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And Allah is ever Muqit over all things﴾. Concerning it there are five interpretations. One: it means Muqtadir (Capable, Powerful), and this is the saying of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The second: Hafiz (Preserver, Guardian), and this is the saying of Ibn Abbas and al-Zajjaj.

The third: Shahid (Witness), and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The fourth: Hasib (Reckoner), and this is the saying of Ibn al-Hajjaj, and it is also related from Mujahid.

The fifth: Mujazi (Recompenser). The original meaning of muqit is qut (sustenance), and the one capable of giving sustenance was named by it, then it became a name for everyone capable over everything, whether sustenance or otherwise, as al-Zubayr ibn Abd al-Muttalib said:

"And one with rancor whom I restrained myself from, and I was capable (muqit) of his harm."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with better than it or return it﴾. Regarding the meaning of greeting (tahiyyah) here there are two opinions. The first: it is the supplication for long life.

The second: it is salam (the greeting of peace). Initiating it is recommended (mustahabb), while returning it is obligatory (fard). Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: the obligation of returning it is general, applying to the Muslim and the disbeliever, and this is the saying of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is specific to Muslims and not to the disbeliever, and this is the saying of Ata.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with better than it﴾ means an increase in the supplication.

﴿or return it﴾ means with its like. al-Hasan narrated that a man greeted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: "As-salamu alaykum," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wa alaykumu s-salam wa rahmatullah." Then another came and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wa alaykumu s-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh." Then another came and said: "As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Wa alaykum." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, you returned to the first and the second, and you said to the third only 'Wa alaykum'?" He said: "The first greeted and left nothing of the greeting, so I returned to him with better than what he brought. Likewise the second. And the third brought the whole greeting, so I returned to him its like."

Ibn Abbas said: "You return with better than it to the people of Islam, or with its like to the people of disbelief." And it has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not initiate greeting the Jews; if they initiate to you, then say: 'Alaykum.'"

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Hasib over all things﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. One: it means Hafiz (Preserver), and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: Muhasib (Reckoner) for deeds, for the sake of recompense for them, and this is the saying of some of the theologians (mutakallimun).

The third: Kafi (Sufficient), and this is the saying of al-Balkhi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection﴾. Concerning the naming of the Resurrection (al-qiyamah) there are two opinions. The first: because people stand (yaqumun) therein from their graves.

The second: because they stand therein for the reckoning.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 88–91:

Allah's words: ﴿So what is [the matter] with you regarding the hypocrites, [that you have become] two groups?﴾ Scholars differed about the occasion of the revelation of this verse, giving five opinions. First: it was revealed concerning those who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud, saying, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." This is the view of Zayd ibn Thabit.

Second: it was revealed concerning a people who came to Madinah and showed Islam, then returned to Makkah and showed polytheism. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

Third: it was revealed concerning a people who showed Islam in Makkah and used to assist the polytheists against the Muslims. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

Fourth: it was revealed concerning a people from the people of Madinah who wanted to leave it out of hypocrisy. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Fifth: it was revealed concerning a people from among the people of the slander (al-Ifk). This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Regarding Allah's words: ﴿And Allah has reverted them [to disbelief] for what they have earned﴾, there are five interpretations. First: its meaning is "He returned them" (radda-hum); this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Second: "He caused them to fall" (awqa'a-hum); this is also related from Ibn Abbas.

Third: "He destroyed them" (ahlaka-hum); this is the view of Qatadah.

Fourth: "He misguided them" (adalla-hum); this is the view of al-Suddi.

Fifth: "He overturned them" (nakkasa-hum); this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾ Scholars differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, giving two views. The first is that it was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi, who was the maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl. He killed al-Harith ibn Zayd from Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, because al-Harith used to torture 'Ayyash along with Abu Jahl. There was also a difference about where he killed him. 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: he killed him at al-Harra after his migration to Madina, while he did not know of his Islam. al-Suddi said: he killed him on the day of the Conquest (of Makkah), after he had left Makkah, while he did not know of his Islam.

The second view is that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Darda', when "he killed a man in al-Sh'b. The man came at him with a sword, and said: 'There is no god but Allah,' but he hastened and struck him down. Then he felt remorse in himself, so he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him about it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did you not split open his heart?'" This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Then Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.﴾ That is, Allah did not permit a believer to kill a believer.

Then He said: ﴿except by mistake.﴾ That is, a believer may kill a believer by mistake, and this is not something Allah has made permissible for him. This is from the exception that the people of Arabic grammar call al-istithna' al-munqati' (the disconnected exception, where the excepted item is not of the same category as what precedes it). From it is the verse of Jarir:

"From the fair ones, she did not travel far, nor did she tread upon the earth except the striped hem of a woven cloak."

That is, she did not tread upon the earth, except that she trod upon the hem of the cloak, and the cloak is not part of the earth.

﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, (the penalty is) the freeing of a believing slave﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first is that a slave may not be freed for the expiation (kaffara) unless she is a believer who has reached maturity and has prayed and fasted. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibrahim.

The second view is that a young child born to two Muslim parents is considered a believer, and her freeing counts for the expiation. This is the view of 'Ata' and al-Shafi'i.

﴿and a compensation (diyya) paid to his family﴾. Regarding the diyya there are two aspects. The first is that it is general (mujmala), and its details were taken from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The second is that it was already known (ma'huda), its practice had already been established, and then the address was directed to it. So Allah made the freeing of a slave an expiation for the killer from his own property, and made the diyya a substitute for the life of the one killed, to be borne by his 'aqila (paternal kinsmen).

﴿But if he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then (the penalty is) the freeing of a believing slave﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: that is, if his people were disbelievers and he was a believer, then killing him requires the freeing of a believing slave, and there is no diyya. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd.

Ibn Zayd said: it is not to be paid to them, because they would strengthen themselves by it.

The second: its meaning is, "if he was from a people hostile to you," that is, people at war with you, and among them there was a believer who was killed without knowledge of his faith, then there is the expiation but not the diyya, whether his heir was a Muslim or a disbeliever. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. In this case the meaning of "from a people" is "from a people to a people." According to the first view, the words are used in their literal sense.

Then Allah said: ﴿But if he was from a people between whom and you there is a covenant, then (the penalty is) a compensation paid to his family and the freeing of a believing slave.﴾ Regarding them there are three views. The first: they are the protected people (ahl al-dhimma) from among the People of the Book. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: the diyya and the expiation are obligatory for killing them.

The second: they are the people of the covenant of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from among the Arabs specifically. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: they are everyone who has a guarantee of safety by protection (dhimma) or by a covenant (ahd), so the diyya and the expiation are obligatory for killing him. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

Then Allah said: ﴿But whoever cannot find (a slave), then (he must fast) two consecutive months﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: fasting is a substitute for the slave alone when he is not available, not for the diyya. This is the view of the majority.

The second: fasting is a substitute for both the slave and the diyya together when they are unavailable. This is the view of Masruq.

Allah's words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning Maqis ibn Subaba. He was a man from Banu Fihr who had killed his brother. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave him the diyya and imposed it upon Banu al-Najjar, so he accepted it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Maqis ibn Subaba with al-Fihri on some errand. Maqis overpowered al-Fihri, who was strong, struck him against the ground, and crushed his head between two stones. Then he recited, singing:

"I killed Fihr by it, and the chiefs of Banu al-Najjar carried his blood-money, the lords of Fari'."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I think he has committed an offence. By Allah, if he has done this, I will not grant him safety in the sacred precinct or outside it." So he was killed on the day of the Conquest.

Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell" (the verse). It was said to him: "And if he repents, believes and does righteous deeds?" He said: "And how would he have repentance?" Zayd ibn Thabit said: then the severe (verse) was revealed six months after the truce, namely His words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾, after His words: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

Then Allah said: ﴿But whoever cannot find (a slave), then (he must fast) two consecutive months﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: fasting is a substitute for the slave alone when he is not available, not for the diyya. This is the view of the majority.

The second: fasting is a substitute for both the slave and the diyya together when they are unavailable. This is the view of Masruq.

Allah's words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning Maqis ibn Subaba. He was a man from Banu Fihr who had killed his brother. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave him the diyya and imposed it upon Banu al-Najjar, so he accepted it. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Maqis ibn Subaba with al-Fihri on some errand. Maqis overpowered al-Fihri, who was strong, struck him against the ground, and crushed his head between two stones. Then he recited, singing:

"I killed Fihr by it, and the chiefs of Banu al-Najjar carried his blood-money, the lords of Fari'."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I think he has committed an offence. By Allah, if he has done this, I will not grant him safety in the sacred precinct or outside it." So he was killed on the day of the Conquest.

Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell" (the verse). It was said to him: "And if he repents, believes and does righteous deeds?" He said: "And how would he have repentance?" Zayd ibn Thabit said: then the severe (verse) was revealed six months after the truce, namely His words: ﴿And whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever﴾, after His words: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 94:

Allah's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you go forth in the way of Allah, investigate carefully﴾ and so on.

It was said: it was revealed concerning a man who had some small goats. A detachment (sariyyah) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ encountered him, and he said to them: "Peace be upon you, there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." But some of them rushed at him and killed him. When he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said to him: "Why did you kill him when he had embraced Islam?" He said: "He only said it out of fear." He said: "Did you not split open his heart to see whether he was sincere?" Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had his blood-money (diyah) paid to his family and returned his goats to them.

The killer was disputed over in five opinions. The first: he was Usamah ibn Zayd, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: he was al-Miqdad, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: Abu al-Darda', and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: Amir ibn al-Adbat al-Ashja'i, and this is the view of Ibn Umar.

The fifth: he was Muhallam ibn Jaththamah al-Laythi.

It is said that the earth rejected the killer three times, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the earth would accept one who is worse than him, but Allah made him a lesson for you," then he commanded that stones be thrown upon him. ﴿Thus you were before﴾, that is, disbelievers like them.

﴿Then Allah bestowed His favour upon you﴾, meaning through Islam.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 95–100:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find on the earth many refuges and abundance﴾. Regarding al-muraghamun (refuge, a place of escape from one's enemies), there are five interpretations. The first: it is the one who moves from one land to another land, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

From it is the saying of Nabigha Bani Jaʿda:

؎ Like a mountain sheltered by its sides, mighty in its refuge and its seeking

The second: it is the seeking of livelihood (matlab al-maʿisha), and this is the view of al-Suddi. From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ To a land not near in its abode ∗∗∗ far in its refuge and its seeking

The third: that al-muraghamu is the place of emigration (al-muhajar), and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: by al-muraghamu is meant a wide space (manduha) away from what one dislikes.

The fifth: that one finds something by which to humiliate them (yurghimuhum bihi), because everyone who departs from his people out of aversion to them has humbled them (arghamahum). This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The root of this is al-rughm, which means humiliation (al-dhull).

Al-raghām means dust, because it is lowly; and al-rughām, with a dammah on the rāʾ, is what flows from the nose.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: (wa saʿatan), there are three interpretations. The first: abundance in provision, and this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: meaning from misguidance to guidance and from poverty to wealth, and this is the saying of Qatadah.

The third: abundance in the manifestation of the religion.

(p-523) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you travel through the land﴾ means you journey, because one who travels strikes the earth with his feet in his journeying just as he strikes it with his hand. For this reason, travel through the land was called "ḍarb" (striking).

﴿There is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear that those who disbelieve may afflict you﴾. Scholars differed regarding this shortening that is conditioned on fear, into two opinions:

One of them: it is the shortening of its pillars (arkān) when one fears, while the number of its units (a'dād) is kept complete. So he prays during close combat and the clash of battle however he is able, standing, sitting, or gesturing (mūmiyan). This is like His saying: ﴿But if you fear, then on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 239]. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: it is the shortening of its number of units (a'dād) from four down to fewer. Regarding this there are three sayings:
The first: this is conditioned on fear, from four to two units. If one is secure and resident, he does not shorten. This is the view of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī.

The second: there are two kinds of shortening: the shortening of security, from four to two units, and the shortening of fear, from two units to one. This is the view of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and al-Ḥasan.

Mujāhid narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, prescribed through the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ) four units in residence, two units in travel, and one unit in fear."

The third: one shortens in travel, whether fearing or secure, from four to two units, and no more.

It is narrated from Abū Ayyūb, from ʿAlī (peace be upon him), who said: "A group of merchants asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, we strike through the land, so how should we pray?' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾. Then revelation ceased. When a year had passed after that, the Prophet (ﷺ) went out on a campaign and prayed the noon prayer. The polytheists said: 'Muhammad and his companions had an opportunity to strike them from behind; why did you not press upon them?' One of them said: 'Indeed they have another prayer after it, equal to it.' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed between the two prayers: ﴿If you fear that those who disbelieve may afflict you. Indeed, the disbelievers are to you a manifest enemy﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾. Then the prayer of fear was revealed."

(p-524)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 4, Verse 102:**

Allah's words: ﴿And when you are among them and establish the prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you [in prayer]﴾. This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he should pray in a state of fear (*salat al-khawf*, the prayer of fear) with his companions.

The scholars differed over whether this ruling was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), according to two opinions. The first is that it is specific to him, and that others of his community may not pray in fear in the same manner as he did, because the polytheists had resolved to attack the Muslims while they were occupied with their prayer. Allah informed His Prophet of their intentions and commanded him to take precautions against them. This was the cause of the conversion to Islam of Khalid ibn al-Walid, and for this reason this ruling became specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). This opinion is reported from Abu Yusuf.

The second opinion is that this ruling is general, applying to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to others of his community when they are in the same circumstances of fear as he was, because mentioning the cause, which is fear, requires that the ruling be applied wherever that cause exists, as the companions did after him when they feared. This is the opinion of the majority (*al-jumhur*).

As for Allah's words ﴿let a group of them stand with you﴾, this means with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the prayer, while another group stands facing the enemy.

Then Allah said ﴿and let them take their weapons﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first is that those commanded to take up arms are those who are with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

The second is that they are those facing the enemy, who guard. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. (p-525)

Then Allah said ﴿and when they have prostrated﴾, meaning when the group that is with you in the prayer has prostrated.

﴿then let them be behind you﴾, meaning facing the enemy.

They differed over Allah's words ﴿behind you﴾: is this after they have finished the prayer and completed it with the *rak'a* (unit of prayer) which they caught with him? There are two opinions. The first is that the prayer is completed by that *rak'a*, so that they pray with him another *rak'a* after the imam finishes. This is the view of those who made the prayer of fear obligatory as two *rak'as*.

Those who held this view differed over whether they complete the remaining *rak'a* before taking up their position facing the enemy or after it, according to two opinions. The first is before taking up position facing the enemy; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. The second is after it; this is the view of Abu Hanifa.

Then Allah said ﴿and let another group come who have not prayed, and let them pray with you﴾. He means that the group facing the enemy comes and prays with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the *rak'a* that remains for him, while the group which has prayed departs and takes its position facing the enemy.

When they pray with the Prophet (ﷺ) the remaining *rak'a*, there are two opinions concerning it. The first is that this is their obligation and they conclude with his *taslim* (salutation ending the prayer). This is the view of those who made their obligation in fear one *rak'a*.

The second opinion is that they have one more *rak'a* to complete, and this is the view of those who made their obligation in fear two *rak'as*, like the prayer of security. According to this view, when do they separate from him? There are two opinions: the first is before his *tashahhud* (the sitting in which the testimony of faith is recited), and the second is after it. Sahl ibn Abi Hathma reported both opinions together from the Prophet (ﷺ). (p-526)

Do they complete their remaining *rak'a* before taking up position facing the enemy? There are two opinions. The first is that they complete it before taking up position facing the enemy; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. The second is that they take up position facing the enemy before completing it, so that when the first group has completed its *rak'a*, it returns and takes up position facing the enemy, and then this group goes out and completes its *rak'a*. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

This prayer is roughly like the prayer of the Prophet (ﷺ) at Dhat al-Riqa' (the battle of Dhat al-Riqa').

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 103–104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when you have finished the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on your sides﴾. He means the remembrance of Allah through glorifying Him, extolling Him, and sanctifying Him after the prayer, whether in fear or otherwise. Ibn 'Abbas said: No one is excused from leaving it except one whose intellect has been overcome.

﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it means, when you are settled after travel, then complete the prayer without shortening it. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid.

The second: its meaning is, when you are secure after your fear, then complete the bowing and prostration without signalling with the head and without walking. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿Indeed, the prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: that is, an obligatory duty. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: it means prescribed at its appointed times and its stars (nujum), whenever one star sets, another comes. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Zayd ibn Aslam.

﴿And do not weaken in pursuit of the enemy﴾. That is, do not be feeble in seeking them out for battle. (p-527)

﴿If you are suffering, then indeed they suffer as you suffer﴾. That is, whatever harm reaches them from you, they suffer from it as you suffer from what reaches you from them.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿but you hope from Allah what they do not hope﴾. That is, this is an additional advantage for you over them and a virtue specific to you to the exclusion of them, despite equality in pain.

Concerning this hope there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that you hope for the victory of Allah which they do not hope for.

The second: you fear from Allah what they do not fear. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not attribute to Allah due dignity?﴾ [Nuh: 31], that is, you do not fear Allah's majesty.

From this is the saying of the poet:

Do not hope when you meet the defender, whether seven have met together or one.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 4, verses 105–115:

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ may carry three meanings. First: the Book is true. Second: it contains mention of the truth. Third: you are most deserving of it.

﴿That you may judge among the people by what Allah has shown you﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: by what Allah has informed you is true. The second: by what your ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) leads you to conclude is true.

﴿And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾, that is, do not dispute on their behalf. This verse was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, and there is disagreement about the occasion of its revelation regarding him. Al-Suddi said: he had been entrusted with a coat of mail and some food, and he denied it, and there was no bayyina (clear evidence) against him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was inclined to defend him, so Allah the Exalted made his case clear.

Al-Hasan said: he had stolen a coat of mail and some food, then denied it and accused someone else, and placed the items in that man's home. A group of the Ansar supported him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) argued on his behalf, or was inclined to do so. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse concerning them, up to His statement: ﴿then he throws it upon an innocent person﴾, meaning the one whom the thief accused and upon whom he placed the theft.

It was also said: he was a man from the Jews called Yazid ibn al-Samin. (p. 529)

It was also said: rather, he was a man from the Ansar called Labid ibn Sahl.

It was also said: Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq apostatized, and this verse was revealed concerning him.

He joined the polytheists of Makkah, and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning him: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers – We will give him what he has turned to﴾ (An-Nisa 4:115), and the rest of the verse.

God's words, ﴿They invoke, apart from Him, only females﴾. On this there are four interpretations.

First: the females are al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. This is the view of al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Malik.

Second: they are the idols. In the codex of 'A'isha it reads: "Those you invoke apart from Him are only females."

Third: they are the angels, because the polytheists claimed that they were the daughters of God. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Fourth: they are the lifeless objects that have no spirit, because the "females" of anything are its most worthless part. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

God's words, ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾, mean from faith.

﴿And I will surely arouse their desires﴾ means through prolonged hope in this world, so that they prefer it over the Hereafter.

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely slit the ears of cattle﴾, that is, they will cut them off as offerings (nusuk, sacrificial rites) for their idols, as with the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released) and the sa'iba (a freed animal released for the idols).

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely alter the creation of God﴾. On this there are three interpretations.

First: it means the religion of God. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibrahim.

Second: it refers to the castration of animals. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas and Ikrimah.

Third: it refers to tattooing (al-washm). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "God has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair and those who have it plucked, the women who file their teeth to make them beautiful, who alter the creation of God." (p-530)

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely alter the creation of God﴾. On this there are three interpretations.

First: it means the religion of God. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibrahim.

Second: it refers to the castration of animals. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas and Ikrimah.

Third: it refers to tattooing (al-washm). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "God has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair and those who have it plucked, the women who file their teeth to make them beautiful, who alter the creation of God." (p-530)

God's words, ﴿They invoke, apart from Him, only females﴾. On this there are four interpretations.

First: the females are al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. This is the view of al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Malik.

Second: they are the idols. In the codex of 'A'isha it reads: "Those you invoke apart from Him are only females."

Third: they are the angels, because the polytheists claimed that they were the daughters of God. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Fourth: they are the lifeless objects that have no spirit, because the "females" of anything are its most worthless part. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

God's words, ﴿And I will surely mislead them﴾, mean from faith.

﴿And I will surely arouse their desires﴾ means through prolonged hope in this world, so that they prefer it over the Hereafter.

﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely slit the ears of cattle﴾, that is, they will cut them off as offerings (nusuk, sacrificial rites) for their idols, as with the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released) and the sa'iba (a freed animal released for the idols).

First: it means the religion of God. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibrahim.

Second: it refers to the castration of animals. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas and Ikrimah.

Third: it refers to tattooing (al-washm). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 123–126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾. In the speech there is an implied, omitted element, and its estimated meaning is: "The reward is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book," according to two views. The first: they are the idol-worshippers, and this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: they are the people of Islam, and this is the view of Masruq and al-Suddi.

﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾. The word "su'" (evil) refers to whatever is harmful among the foul deeds, and there are three views concerning it here. The first: that it is associating partners with Allah, exalted is He, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it is the major sins (al-kaba'ir, the grave sins), and this is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

The third: that it is what a person encounters in this world of sorrows and calamities as a recompense for his bad deeds, as Muhammad ibn Qays ibn Makhrama narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims and affected them to the extent that Allah willed, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Be steadfast and aim for correctness, for in everything a Muslim is afflicted with there is an expiation, even the prick he is pricked with or the thorn that pricks him.'" Al-A'mash narrated from Muslim, who said: "Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how severe is this verse: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾!' He said: 'O Abu Bakr, indeed the calamity in this world is a recompense.'"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 127:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them"﴾, and so on.

It has been differed over regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, on two views. One of them: the occasion of its revelation is that in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) they did not give inheritance to women or to children. When Allah, exalted is He, prescribed the inheritance laws in this surah, that weighed heavily on the people, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾. Regarding this there are two views.

One of them: it means the inheritance shares. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they did not give women their dowries (sadaqat), and their guardians (awliya') would take possession of them. When the saying of Allah, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift (nihlah)﴾, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to whom you do not give what has been prescribed for them﴾ means what has been obligated for them of the dowry, and this is the view of 'A'ishah.

﴿and you desire to marry them﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One of them: you turn away from marrying them because of their ugliness.

The second: you keep them out of desire for their wealth and their beauty, and this is the view of 'A'ishah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 128–130:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion﴾ and so on. Scholars differ regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, on two views:

One of them: it was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he intended to divorce Sawda bint Zam'a, so she gave her day to 'A'isha on condition that he not divorce her, and this verse was revealed concerning it.

This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second view: it is general in every woman who fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion.

Nushuz (ill-treatment) is his raising himself above her out of hatred for her, and i'rad (aversion) is that he turns away from inclining towards her due to a grievance or self-preference.

﴿There is no blame upon them both if they make terms of settlement between themselves﴾, either by her forgoing a dowry or relinquishing a turn.

﴿And settlement is best﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: it means better than ill-treatment and aversion, and this is the view of some of the Basran scholars.

The second: better than separation, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿And souls are made present to stinginess﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: the souls of women are made present to stinginess regarding their rights from their husbands and their wealth, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: the soul of each of the man and the woman is made present to stinginess regarding his or her right before the other, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives﴾, meaning in your hearts and your love.

﴿And even if you should strive﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: even if you should strive to be equitable in love, and this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: even if you should strive in intercourse, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿So do not incline completely [away]﴾, meaning do not incline by your actions, so that you follow your desires.

﴿And leave her as in suspension﴾, meaning neither unmarried nor a married woman.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they separate, Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾, meaning the spouses if they separate by divorce.

﴿Allah will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ admits three aspects. One: Allah will enrich each of them by contentment and patience, free from the other, and the meaning of His saying ﴿from His abundance﴾ is from His mercy, for He is vast in mercy.

The second: Allah will enrich each of them, free from the other, with one better than him, and the meaning of His saying ﴿from His abundance﴾ is from His power, for He is vast in power.

The third: Allah will enrich each of them with wealth that is more beneficial to him than his companion, and the meaning of His saying ﴿from His abundance﴾ is from His independence, for He is vast in independence.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 131–134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you, O people, and bring others﴾. Sahl ibn Abi Salih narrated from Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this was revealed, he struck Salman's back with his hand and said: "They are the people of this one," meaning the non-Arab Persians (ʿajam al-Furs).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the reward of this world, with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter﴾. The reward of this world is blessing (niʿmah), and the reward of the Hereafter is Paradise (al-Jannah).
