Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning testimony for them and against them.

﴿And if you distort or turn away﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Hamzah read it with a single waw (تَلُوا), from wilayah (governance), meaning: if you govern the affairs of people or abandon them. This applies to rulers and judges.

The rest of the readers read (تَلْوُوا) with two waws.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it means that a person twists his tongue in testimony, as a man twists another man's debt when he delays paying it. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The procrastination of the wealthy man makes his honor and his punishment lawful." Al-A'sha said:

؎ They delay my debt by day, and I demand my debt when sleep overcomes the sleepers.

On this reading and interpretation, the address is to the witnesses.(p-536)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. It may be asked: how is it said to them, "Believe," when it is related of them that they had believed? There are three answers to this.

The first: "O you who have believed" refers to those who believed in the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ). So "Believe in Allah and His Messenger" is addressed to the Jews and the Christians.

The second: its meaning is, "O you who have believed with your mouths, believe with your hearts." This is addressed to the hypocrites (munafiqun).

The third: its meaning is, "O you who have believed, persevere in your faith." This is addressed to the believers, and this is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 137–140:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and then disbelieved, then believed and then disbelieved﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: They believed in Musa, then disbelieved by worshipping the calf; then they believed in Musa after his return, then disbelieved in ʿIsa, then they increased in disbelief by [rejecting] Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: They are the hypocrites (munafiqun) who believed, then apostatized, then believed, then apostatized, then died upon their disbelief. This is the view of Mujahid.

Third: They are a people from among the People of the Book who intended to cast doubt upon the believers, so they would display faith and then disbelief, then they increased in disbelief by persisting in it. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Scholars differed, on account of this verse, regarding the seeking of repentance (istitabah) from the apostate (murtadd), on two opinions. The first: the apostate is asked to repent three times, based on the indication of the verse; if he apostatizes after the three times, he is killed without being asked to repent again. This is the view of ʿAli.

The second: he is asked to repent every time he apostatizes. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and the majority (al-jumhur).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 141:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who wait [for an opportunity] against you﴾ — meaning the hypocrites.

﴿If you have a victory from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?"﴾ — i.e., give us a share of the spoils of war.

﴿And if the disbelievers have a portion, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you?"﴾ — Concerning this there are three interpretations (ta'wilat). The first: its meaning is, "Did we not gain mastery over you (istawla 'alaykum) through assistance and support, and did we not prevent you from the believers by discouraging them from you?"

The second: its meaning is, "Did we not make clear to you that we are upon your religion?" This is the view of Ibn Juraij.

The third: its meaning is, "Did we not overcome you?" This is the view of al-Suddi.

The origin of istihwaz (gaining mastery) is domination (al-ghalabah), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Satan has gained mastery over them﴾ — meaning, he overcame them.

Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ there are two views (qawlan): (p-538)

The first: it means a proof (hujjah). This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: it means a way in the Hereafter. This is the view of Ali and Ibn Abbas.

The Words of the Exalted and Majestic: "Indeed, the hypocrites deceive Allah, but He is deceiving them" (4:142). The meaning of "they deceive Allah" is: they deceive the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) by displaying faith outwardly while concealing disbelief inwardly. Thus their deceit toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became deceit toward Allah, the Exalted and Majestic.

"But He is deceiving them" means Allah, the Exalted. There are three interpretations of this:

The first: He punishes them for their deceit, so He called the requital of the act by its name (this is an instance of the figure of speech called mushakalah, in which the recompense is named after the deed).

The second: He commanded regarding them the command given to one who is being deceived, namely to accept their profession of faith, even though He knows what disbelief they conceal.

The third: the light He gives them in the Hereafter, by which they walk along with the believers. When they come to the Sirat (the bridge over Hell), their light is extinguished, and that is Allah's deception of them.

"And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily" (4:142). This may carry two meanings:
One: sluggishly, reluctantly.
Two: falling short (in its requirements).

"They show off to the people" (4:142): meaning that in the good deeds they perform, they intend the show-off of people rather than obedience to Allah, the Exalted.

"And they remember Allah only a little" (4:142). There are two opinions regarding this:
One: "a little" means showing off, since it is not remembrance except of a paltry sort. This is the view of Qatadah. (p-539)

The second: "little" means slight, since they confine themselves to what is apparent of takbir and not to what they keep hidden of recitation and glorification. It was little because of their belief, not because of the scarcity of their remembrance.

al-Hasan said: "Because it was for other than Allah, the Exalted."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verses 148–152:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations.

The first: it means, except when one is wronged and so supplicates against the one who wronged him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: except when one is wronged and so openly speaks of the wrong done by the one who wronged him. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: except one who has been wronged and so takes his right from his oppressor. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The fourth: except when one is a guest, who stays with a people and they do not treat him hospitably; then there is no harm in his openly denouncing them. This is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

Then, after permitting the mention of evil in speech for one who has been wronged, He said: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾, meaning: disclose good in place of evil, or conceal the evil. And if you do not disclose good, pardon the evil; this is better and purer, although forgoing pardon is also permissible.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven﴾. On this there are three opinions.

First: the Jews asked Muhammad (ﷺ) to bring down to them a book from heaven in written form, as He had sent down the tablets and the Torah written from heaven to Musa. This is the view of al-Suddi and Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

Second: they asked him to bring this down to them specifically, as an arbitrary demand for signs. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Third: they asked him to bring down a book from heaven to a group of their leaders, attesting to his truth. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

﴿So they asked Musa for something greater than that, and said: Show us God openly﴾. This may bear two meanings. First: by this God the Exalted made clear that their asking was for obstruction, not for insight, just as they asked Musa to show them God openly, and then they disbelieved by worshipping the calf. Second: He made clear that they asked for what was not theirs, just as they asked Musa for what was not theirs.

﴿They said: Show us God openly﴾. On this there are two views. First: they asked him to let them see Him openly, that is, with direct witnessing. Second: they meant, "Openly, in speech: show us God," so the words are in inverted order. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing﴾. On this there are two views. First: for their wrongdoing against themselves. Second: for their wrongdoing in their asking.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We raised above them the mountain for their covenant﴾. That is: by the pact that was taken from them after they affirmed the Torah, that they would act by what is in it. They broke it by worshipping the calf, so God raised the mountain over them so that they would repent, and otherwise it would fall upon them. Then they repented.

﴿And We said to them: Enter the gate prostrating﴾. On this there are two views. First: it is the gate of the place where they worshipped the calf, one of the gates of the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis). This is the view of Qatadah. Second: it is the gate of Hittah, and they were commanded to enter it prostrating to God, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And We said to them: Do not transgress in the Sabbath﴾. Warsh, from Nafi', recited (تَعَدُّوا) with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda on the dal, from the verb al-iʿtidaʾ (to transgress). The rest recited it with the light form from (عَدَوْتَ). Their ʿadw in it is their exceeding its limits. So, according to the second recitation, their transgression in it means abandoning its obligations.

﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾. This is another covenant, after the raising of the mountain over them, distinct from the first covenant.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿solemn﴾, there are two views. First: it is a pact after an oath. Second: some oaths are a solemn covenant.

The Qur'anic verse ﴿And their saying, "Our hearts are wrapped"﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that they are veiled from understanding the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an and the proofs of its truthfulness, as something enclosed in a sheath. This is the view of some of the Basran scholars.

The second is that the hearts are receptacles for knowledge, yet they do not understand your argument or recognise your inimitability. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. On the first interpretation, their words are a form of turning away (i'rad); on the second, they are a form of rejection (ibtal).

﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them over because of their disbelief﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that He placed on them a sign that informs the angels of their disbelief, like the mark on a sealed object. This is the view of some of the Basran scholars.

The second is that He censured them by saying their hearts are like something sealed upon, which never understands and never obeys a guide. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾ has two interpretations:

The first is that a few of them believe in Allah.

The second is that they believe only in a little, namely their belief in some of the prophets rather than all of them.

The Almighty and Majestic said: ﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah"﴾. As for their saying, ﴿"Indeed, we killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam"﴾, it is the saying of the Jews, which Allah reported about them.

As for ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾, there are two interpretations. The first is that it is also the saying of the Jews, meaning "the messenger of Allah" in their claim.

The second is that it is the saying of Allah the Exalted, not as a report about them. Its meaning is: "the one who is My messenger."

﴿But they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ has three interpretations. The first is that they used to know him, so He cast his likeness upon another, and they thought he was the Messiah and killed him. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, Wahb and al-Suddi.

The second is that they did not know him by his person, although he was well known among them by description. A Jew was bribed by them with thirty dirhams, and he pointed them to someone else, giving them the impression that he was the Messiah, so it was made to appear so to them.

The third is that they knew him, but their leaders feared the temptation (fitnah) it would cause among their common people. God prevented them from him, so they turned to someone else, killed him and crucified him, and disguised it to the common people as though he were the Messiah, so that their being led astray by him would end.

﴿And indeed, those who differ concerning him are in doubt about it﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that they differed concerning him before his killing: some said he was a god, some said he was a son, and some said he was a sorcerer, so they doubted. ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption﴾ refers to the doubt that arose among them through their disagreement.

The second is that they have no knowledge of his condition, whether he was a messenger or not, except the following of assumption.

﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾ has three interpretations:

The first is: they did not kill their assumption with certainty, in the manner of someone saying, "I did not kill him with knowledge." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Juwaybir.

The second is: they did not know with certainty the matter of whether the man was the Messiah or someone else. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third is: they did not really kill him. This is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾ has two interpretations. The first is that He raised him to a place where no judgment of any of the servants applies, so his being raised to a place where the judgment of the servants does not apply is his being raised to Him. This is the view of some of the Basran scholars.

The second is that He raised him to the heaven. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The Exalted said: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that they will surely believe in him before his death﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: they will surely believe in the Messiah before the death of the Messiah, when he descends from the heaven. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik, Qatada and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they will surely believe in the Messiah before the death of the People of the Scripture at the moment of witnessing death, so they will believe in what Allah sent down of the truth and in the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam. O people, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord — i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ), because of the miracle that he possesses, which testifies to his truthfulness.

And We have sent down to you a manifest light — meaning the Qur'an. It is called a light because through it the truth becomes manifest, just as visible things become apparent by means of light.

Regarding His saying, ﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him﴾, there are two opinions:
One: they held fast to the Qur'an. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.
The second: they held fast to Allah against the deviation of Satan and the desire of the human self.

﴿Then He will admit them into mercy from Him and bounty and guide them to Himself on a straight path﴾. Concerning the guidance there are two opinions:
One: that He gives them in this world what leads them to the bliss of the Hereafter. This is the view of al-Hasan.
The second: that it is His taking them in the Hereafter along the path to Paradise. This is the view of some of the Basran exegetes.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 4, verse 176:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning al-kalalah"﴾ — the verse.

Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: "The last surah to be revealed in its entirety was Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), and the last verse to be revealed, as the conclusion of Surat al-Nisa', was ﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾."

And Jabir ibn Abd Allah said: "This verse was revealed concerning me. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he visited me during my illness, and I had nine sisters, 'How should I deal with my wealth?' He did not answer me with anything, until there was revealed: ﴿They ask you for a ruling﴾," up to the end of the surah.

Ibn Sirin said: "This verse was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on a journey, and beside him was Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed it to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Hudhayfah conveyed it to Umar ibn al-Khattab, while he was walking behind him."
